paper_title: Predicting Privileged Information Effectiveness for On-Policy Self-Distillation

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) enables large language models (LLMs) to learn from privileged information (PI) without a separate teacher model. However, prior work largely treats PI as a fixed design choice, leaving the effects of its content and construction poorly understood. This challenge is particularly important in multi-turn agentic settings, where trajectories contain actions, observations, and reasoning that can be transformed into PI in many ways. We systematically evaluate 16 PI configurations across three multi-turn agentic benchmarks and three student models that vary in scale and reasoning mode. We find that PI effectiveness depends on its content, generation source, and the student model. Information-dense trajectories and PI produced by more capable generators generally yield larger gains, whereas thinking models benefit less consistently. To assess PI before training, we compare PI utility with two KL-based metrics: sampled-token reverse KL ($D$) and error-step KL contrast ($Δd^{-}_{\mathrm{err}}$). The KL-based metrics track post-training performance more consistently than PI utility, which can be distorted by information leakage. Empirically, selecting each task's PI by $Δd^{-}_{\mathrm{err}}$ also improves post-training performance over random selection, most when the PI candidates differ widely. Finally, effective PI remains beneficial when combined with GRPO, allowing the combined objective to outperform a strong GRPO baseline. Overall, our results provide practical guidance for constructing and evaluating PI in OPSD training.

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) enables LLMs to iteratively improve by turning successful solutions, environment feedback, and experience from their own interactions into training signals without separate teacher model [7, 19, 22, 35]. Related self-distillation methods have already been used to train coding agents such as Composer 2.5 and agents for long-horizon professional tasks [4, 8]. In OPSD, the model learns from its own trajectories by matching the same model conditioned on PI, thereby internalizing information unavailable at inference time. Corresponding authors: zkjzou@umich.edu, anas.mahmoud@scale.com. Work done during an internship at Scale AI.

Error-step KL contrast err measures whether that shift targets the identified errors. The effectiveness of OPSD, however, depends on what the teacher is allowed to see. In general, PI can take many forms, including ground-truth answers [35], demonstrations from prior tasks [22], environment feedback [7], actions from successful trajectories [19], or hints derived from gold solutions or trajectories, such as summaries [19], skills [26], checklists, structured criteria such as rubrics [6, 20], and targeted feedback [4, 33]. These choices determine both the information available to the teacher and how that information changes its distribution relative to the student. However, especially on multi-turn agentic tasks, existing studies evaluate only limited range of PI formats across small set of models and tasks [16, 26, 29, 30, 33]. It remains unclear what makes PI produce useful learning signals for the student policy, whether the same choices work across agentic domains and model types, and, critically, whether PI quality can be assessed before training. Reliable offline metrics would allow candidate PI formats and sources to be compared before training, avoiding separate costly OPSD run for every candidate and focusing compute on the most promising PI. We study these questions through systematic evaluation of OPSD on three multi-turn agentic benchmarks: ALFWorld [24], AppWorld [25], and τ2-retail [2]. Figure 1 summarizes the PI formats and offline metrics evaluated in our study. We cover 16 PI configurations spanning reference trajectories and selfand expert-generated hints, including summaries, skills, and checklists. We train Qwen3-4B-Instruct, Qwen3-4B-Thinking, and Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct [28], allowing us to compare PI effects across instruction and thinking models and across model scales. Beyond downstream performance, we evaluate three offline metrics: PI utility [19] compares teacher reward with and without PI, but can be distorted by information leakage; sampled-token reverse KL measures the PI-induced probability shift on

Together, these experiments ask not only which PI works, but also what distinguishes useful PI from information that merely makes the teacher more capable when PI is present. Our results show that PI effectiveness depends on its content, source, and the student model. PI formats with information-dense trajectories usually outperform compressed hints, and adding environment observations consistently improves the Instruct students on ALFWorld and AppWorld. Additional teacher reasoning is less reliable and can reduce the gains of the thinking models. Among hint formats, skills are generally strongest, suggesting that additional guidance, such as an analysis of mistakes and reusable strategies, is more effective than plain trajectory summary. More capable generators also tend to produce more effective PI, particularly for hint formats, showing that PI quality depends on both its format and source. Among the three offline metrics, error-step KL contrast better distinguishes useful PI and improves per-task selection when PI candidates vary in source or strength. Sampled-token reverse KL tracks performance in eight of nine settings but does not capture the direction of the shift, while PI utility is unreliable because of information leakage (Figure 3). Our controlled evaluations on ALFWorld also show that PI utility can be distorted by information leakage and that reverse KL can assign large values to unhelpful shifts. Using the most effective PI format, we further show that combining OPSD with GRPO can outperform strong GRPO baseline. Our main contributions are: Systematic study of PI for OPSD. To our knowledge, this is the first controlled study of PI construction for OPSD, spanning 16 PI configurations and three student models across three multi-turn agentic benchmarks. Practical PI design recommendations. We identify how PI content, format, generation source, and student-model choice shape OPSD gains. KL-based PI assessment and selection. We propose two offline KL diagnostics, evaluate what they measure through controlled studies, and show that error-step KL contrast can guide per-task PI selection before costly OPSD training. Combining OPSD with GRPO. We show that the most effective PI enables combined OPSD and GRPO training to outperform matched GRPO baselines.

sections.title: 2.3 Experimental Setup
sections.content: We evaluate OPSD on ALFWorld [24], AppWorld [25], and τ2-retail [2], using Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507, Qwen3-4B-Thinking-2507, and Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507 as students. We implement OPSD in SkyRL [3] with the sampled-token reverse-KL objective and report pass@1 from the best three-checkpoint window. Offline metrics are computed on training or development tasks disjoint from the evaluation sets used to measure post-training performance. Appendices and provide the benchmark splits, sampling protocols, training hyperparameters, and evaluation settings.

sections.title: 3.2 What Do PI Metrics Reveal?
sections.content: Given the variation across PI configurations above and the substantial cost of training each one, we next ask whether post-training effectiveness can be assessed without running OPSD for every candidate. Figure 3 plots each PI metric against post-training performance for every student under each PI configuration across ALFWorld, AppWorld, and τ2-retail. All diagnostics are computed on training or development tasks disjoint from the post-training evaluation sets. These comparisons show how utility, the distributional-shift statistic D, and the error-step contrast err relate to the performance gains produced by different PI configurations. PI utility can be inflated by information leakage. The PI utility measures the improvement in the success rate of model when conditioned on given PI. We find that this metric can reward PI that reveals answer-specific information unavailable to the student, rather than PI that provides transferable training signal. On AppWorld, the utility metric correlates strongly with post-training performance for all three students (ρ = 0.810.96). The relationship is less consistent on ALFWorld, where the correlation is positive for 4B-Instruct (ρ = 0.46) but negative for 4B-Thinking and 30B-Instruct (ρ = 0.56 and 0.10), and on τ2, where correlations range from 0.06 to 0.71. On ALFWorld, the PI-conditioned model can copy the reference trajectorys final action without reproducing the preceding interaction sequence. On τ2, it can extract an answer from PI without executing the actions required to update the environments database (Appendix D). In these cases, utility measures the models ability to exploit leaked solution information rather than how well the PI transfers through training. Takeaway. PI utility is unreliable when information leakage changes evaluation behavior without providing transferable guidance, so higher utility does not imply larger OPSD gains. Larger distributional shifts usually accompany better performance. We next examine D, the mean absolute sampled-token reverse KL between the student and PI-conditioned teacher. It correlates positively with post-training performance in eight of the nine studentbenchmark combinations (ρ = 0.650.95). The exception is 4B-Thinking on τ2, where the correlation is strongly negative (ρ = 0.84). Its pass@4 of 88.9 suggests that large shift can overwrite useful behavior already present in the policy. Our PI ablations point the same way: the students own failed rollouts induce larger than its successful ones, even though they make far worse PI (Appendix E). Thus, shift direction and location matter in addition to magnitude. Takeaway. larger generally indicates stronger PI training signal, but does not reveal whether the induced shift improves the policy.

sections.title: 4.1 Combined Training Objective
sections.content: Rather than optimizing over the many possible ways to combine token-level distillation and GRPO outcome rewards [21], we use simple weighted objective to test whether PI identified as effective under vanilla OPSD remains effective when combined with GRPO. We use Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 for all experiments in this section. We combine the GRPO and OPSD signals at the advantage level: AOPSD+GRPO = λAGRPO + (1 λ)AOPSD, (7) where AGRPO is the outcome-based group-relative advantage, AOPSD is the token-level self-distillation advantage, and λ [0, 1] controls their relative weight. Figure 4 compares four values of λ across three PI formats with matched GRPO-only controls on ALFWorld, AppWorld, and τ2. The λ = 0 endpoint corresponds to vanilla OPSD.

sections.title: 4.2 Effect of Objective Weighting
sections.content: PI quality persists: better PI is still better after adding GRPO. Trajectory PI performs best under vanilla OPSD and remains strongest across most values of λ, followed by Skill and Checklist PI. This ordering is consistent through λ = 0.99 on all benchmarks. Thus, combining OPSD with outcome-based rewards does not eliminate differences in PI quality: stronger PI continues to provide more effective auxiliary training signal.

sections.title: Scale AI Research
sections.content: Takeaway. The PI format that performs best under vanilla OPSD generally remains the strongest after adding GRPO, so outcome rewards complement rather than replace effective PI selection. GRPO strengthens OPSD. Increasing λ generally improves performance for all three PI formats, with the largest gains occurring for the weaker Checklist and Skill formats on ALFWorld and AppWorld. On ALFWorld, several Skill and Trajectory configurations exceed the GRPO-only baseline score, with Trajectory PI reaching 95.13 at λ = 0.99 versus the baseline score of 84.96. On AppWorld, Trajectory PI at λ = 0.99 reaches 43.90, exceeding the GRPO score of 42.91. Likewise, on τ2, it reaches 55.04, compared with 48.27 for GRPO. Takeaway. Increasing the GRPO weight substantially improves vanilla OPSD. With strong PI and appropriate weighting, the combined objective can outperform matched GRPO baseline. PI improves sample efficiency, but its benefit fades once the policy has learned from it. The training curves in Figure 4 show that PI-guided training, particularly with Trajectory PI, improves rapidly during the initial steps. On ALFWorld, all three PI-guided curves plateau or decline after step 100, corresponding to one epoch, while GRPO continues to improve. This suggests that PI provides its largest optimization benefit early in training, before the policy has learned the information it can readily extract from PI. Because each training task uses the same static PI throughout training, its supervision may become redundant after the first epoch. Beyond this point, the OPSD signal can become distraction that interferes with further outcome-based learning. On AppWorld, Trajectory PI reaches nearly 100% training success at λ = 0.9 but only 39.14 test pass@1, suggesting that this improved sample efficiency can also accelerate overfitting on small, less diverse training sets. Takeaway. PI accelerates early learning, especially when it contains strong reference trajectory. Its marginal benefit decreases after the policy has learned the most readily transferable behavior, after which continued OPSD can even hinder further improvement.

sections.title: 5 Which Offline Metric Should Guide PI Choice?
sections.content: We complement the observational analysis of Section 3.2 with two controlled evaluations of the offline PI metrics. ALFWorld-Passcode isolates the effect of leaked information (Section 5.1), and per-task selection evaluates whether the KL metrics can identify effective PI from candidate pools (Section 5.2); Appendix reports additional ablations with corrupted and length-matched PI. Together, these studies further demonstrate the limitations of utility and how error-step KL contrast can guide PI selection in practice. Finally, we provide practical recommendations for using the proposed KL metrics. All experiments train Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 with vanilla OPSD on ALFWorld and report held-out pass@1, following Section 2.3.

sections.title: 5.3 Practical Recommendations
sections.content: We recommend using the proposed KL metrics, and error-step KL contrast in particular when candidate PI quality is inconsistent, to select PI likely to perform well under vanilla OPSD, then combining it with

sections.content: a strong GRPO signal to accelerate early learning. Once the benefit of PI plateaus, its weight should be reduced or removed to avoid interfering with further outcome-based learning. Another direction is to construct new PI that targets the trained models remaining errors, allowing it to benefit from updated supervision rather than repeatedly training on the same static PI. Providing multiple diverse PI instances per task may offer similar benefit. On small training sets, the PI schedule and diversity should be selected using held-out performance rather than training success alone.

sections.title: 6 Related Work
sections.content: On-policy self-distillation and PI construction. Conventional language-model distillation often trains student on sequences generated by the teacher, whereas on-policy distillation (OPD) supervises student-generated trajectories on the students own state distribution [1, 31]. OPSD removes the need for separate teacher by conditioning the student on PI. Prior OPSD methods use verified answers or reasoning traces [35], environment feedback [7], continual-learning demonstrations [22], and successful agent trajectories [19]. More targeted constructions include skills and mistake analyses [26], hindsight feedback [33], and structured rubrics [6, 20]. However, PI-conditioned supervision can transfer undesirable context effects, reduce output diversity, suppress uncertainty expression, or disrupt self-correction in thinking models [9, 11, 13, 17]. Its effectiveness also depends on the PI representation, student, and sampled rollouts [34]. We compare PI content, source, and student model under shared protocol to identify what explains downstream effectiveness across PI configurations. Combining OPSD with reinforcement learning. Outcome-based RL provides reliable task-level objective, whereas OPSD can supply denser token-level guidance. Recent methods combine these signals in different ways. RLSD uses self-distillation to determine token-level update magnitudes while retaining RLVR rewards to determine the update direction [29]. SRPO routes successful samples to GRPO and failed samples to entropy-weighted self-distillation [14], while RLCSD contrasts the teacherstudent gaps induced by correct and incorrect PI to suppress PI-induced style shifts [18]. For agents, Skill-SD stabilizes joint learning from skills and rewards [26], and SDAR uses OPSD as gated auxiliary objective to an RL backbone [16]. OPID and SEED construct hierarchical or evolving skills from on-policy trajectories and distill them jointly with outcome-based RL [27, 30]. RLRT instead reverses the teacher signal on successful rollouts to reinforce correct reasoning paths not favored by the teacher [10]. We study simple weighted combination of GRPO and OPSD, isolating whether and how their supervision signals complement each other.

sections.title: 7 Conclusion
sections.content: This work provides controlled study of how privileged information shapes on-policy self-distillation across 16 PI configurations, three agentic benchmarks, and three student models. The results show that effective PI must provide more than correct solution. Environment observations, mistake-aware strategies, and detailed reference trajectories often improve learning, and more capable generators generally produce stronger PI. However, these benefits depend on the student: thinking models benefit less consistently, particularly when long reasoning traces make supervision difficult to target at actual errors. PI effectiveness can also be assessed before committing to costly policy training. PI utility is unreliable because leaked information can alter teacher performance without transferring to the student. The

sections.title: Scale AI Research
sections.content: proposed KL metrics instead measure how PI changes the student distribution: sampled-token reverse KL captures the magnitude of this shift, while error-step KL contrast captures whether it is directed toward identified mistakes. Their stronger relationship with post-training performance makes them useful for screening PI formats and sources before running OPSD. Selecting each tasks PI by error-step KL contrast also improves over random selection, whereas selecting by reverse KL can favor misleading PI. Finally, PI selection remains important when OPSD is combined with GRPO. Strong PI can improve upon matched GRPO baselines and accelerate early learning, but static PI may become redundant as training progresses and can encourage overfitting on small datasets. Future work should explore diverse PI instances and adaptive schedules that reduce or reshape the distillation signal as the student learns. Overall, effective PI is distinguished not by how much it helps the teacher solve task, but by whether it produces strong, error-targeted learning signal for the student.

sections.title: A PI Construction
sections.content: Reference trajectories. For every training task of each benchmark, we sample rollouts from GLM-5.2 and Qwen3.7-Plus in the training environment and keep one successful rollout per task and model, recording its actions, the observations returned by the environment, and the models reasoning. Both models are queried through the Fireworks API with its default sampling parameters. Trajectory formats. The four trajectory formats render reference trajectory at different levels of detail: Action keeps only the actions, Action + Obs. adds the observation that follows each action, Action + Thou. adds the reasoning that precedes each action, and Action + Obs. + Thou. keeps both. Hints. Each hint is written by hint generator (GLM-5.2, Qwen3.7-Plus, or the student itself for Self ) from GLM-5.2 reference trajectories: Summary: given one successful GLM-5.2 trajectory, the generator writes short plain-text summary of the key actions and strategy (prompt in Appendix H.2.1). Skill: given one successful GLM-5.2 trajectory, the generator writes success analysis, mistake analysis and an abstract workflow, rendered as recommended approach and key skill (prompts in Appendix H.2.2). Checklist: given one successful GLM-5.2 trajectory paired with one failed trajectory of the student on the same task, the generator writes the pre-action checklist that would have carried the failed attempt to success (prompts in Appendix H.2.3). Summaries and skills are generated at temperature 0.7 and checklists at temperature 0.3. Example hints for one training task per benchmark are shown in Appendix H.3.

sections.title: D How Information Leakage Distorts PI Utility
sections.content: PI utility (Equation 2) places the PI in the models own prompt at inference and measures the resulting change in success. This setup gives the evaluated model direct access to information unavailable to the student after distillation. We study this effect on ALFWorld and τ2-retail and find that leaked information can either increase performance through shortcuts or decrease it by distracting the model. Consequently, utility can reflect how the model uses PI in context rather than the training signal that PI provides in OPSD, where only the teacher observes PI. ALFWorld: the model copies the goal-completing action. Every trajectory hint ends on the reference agents final action, which is always the one that completes the goal (e.g., placing the object in its destination). Given such hint, the model often takes this action first, as if it were already in the final state and one step from success. Its preconditions are not yet met (e.g., the agent is not holding the object), so the environment answers Nothing happens. An Action hint is list numbered from step 1, and the model follows it in order instead. Nearly every such first action fails, and the model issues the final action at least twice in 5195% of the rollouts under the longer formats, against 312% under Action. sections.title: E PI Ablations
sections.content: To see how the three offline metrics react when the PI is corrupted, we ablate the PI (Figure 7): Mismatched gives each task the Action + Obs. + Thou. trajectory of different training task. Other domain gives each task trajectory from τ2-retail or AppWorld. Wrong self gives each task one of the students own failed rollouts. As control for length, Action (padded) repeats the original action list until it is as long as its full trajectory. All three metrics flag mismatched and other-domain PI. Both corruptions remove most of the benefit of OPSD: compared with 87.9 pass@1 for the tasks own trajectory, mismatched PI reaches 34.8, and other-domain PI degrades the student to 5.4, below the untrained student baseline. Utility, D, and err all place both PIs below the two references, and other-domain PI scores the lowest on all three. wrong PI can still produce large shift. The students failed rollouts yield poor OPSD performance, which utility flags because they offer little help in context. Yet they shift the teacher about as much as successful self-rollouts, while error-step KL contrast is much lower for them. On the tasks of the self-rollout selection pools (Appendix F), failed rollouts even have larger than successful ones but lower err. large shift alone therefore does not indicate useful PI, explaining why selection by favors failed rollouts in Section 5.2. PI length is not the main driver of the KL metrics. Padding the action list to the length of the full trajectory changes and err only slightly, and OPSD performance stays close to that of the unpadded action list. The larger shift of trajectory PIs appears to reflect their content more than their length.
